blocks.text: A percentile tells you the value below which a given percentage of a dataset falls. Saying a score is in the 90th percentile means 90 percent of scores in the comparison group were lower, a way of describing position within a dataset that goes well beyond the single middle value the median provides.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What a Percentile Means

The k-th percentile of a dataset is the value below which k percent of the data points fall. A student scoring in the 80th percentile on a standardized test did better than 80 percent of everyone else who took it, regardless of their raw numeric score.

Percentiles describe relative position, not an absolute quality judgment, a good raw score in a very strong group of test takers can still correspond to a lower percentile than a mediocre raw score in a weaker group.
Percentiles always range from 0 to 100, with the 0th percentile being the minimum value in the dataset and the 100th percentile being the maximum.
2. Computing a Percentile

To find the k-th percentile by hand, sort the data, then locate the position (k divided by 100) times (n minus 1), where n is the number of values, using linear interpolation between the two nearest sorted values if that position is not a whole number.

code.content:
import numpy as np
data = [12, 15, 14, 10, 18, 20, 11]
p90 = np.percentile(data, 90)
print(p90)   # interpolated 90th percentile value

blocks.text: Different libraries and even different settings within the same library can use slightly different interpolation conventions, which is why two tools can occasionally report marginally different percentile values for the exact same dataset.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: For 7 sorted values, the 90th percentile position works out to roughly 5.4, meaning the true 90th percentile is interpolated between the 5th and 6th sorted values, closer to the 6th, rather than landing exactly on any single observed value.

blocks.text: 3. The Median as the 50th Percentile

The median, covered in its own lesson, is exactly the 50th percentile, the value below which half the data falls. Every formula and intuition already built for the median transfers directly into the broader percentile framework as the special case where k equals 50.

code.content:
median_val = np.median(data)
p50_val = np.percentile(data, 50)
print(median_val, p50_val)   # identical

blocks.text: This equivalence is a useful check, if a computed median and a computed 50th percentile ever disagree on the same dataset, something in one of the two calculations has gone wrong.
4. Quartiles

Quartiles split a dataset into four equal parts. The first quartile, Q1, is the 25th percentile, the second quartile, Q2, is the 50th percentile and therefore the median, and the third quartile, Q3, is the 75th percentile.

code.content:
q1 = np.percentile(data, 25)
q2 = np.percentile(data, 50)
q3 = np.percentile(data, 75)
print(q1, q2, q3)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quartile","Percentile","Meaning"],"rows":[["Q1","25th","25 percent of values fall below this point"],["Q2","50th","the median, the middle of the dataset"],["Q3","75th","75 percent of values fall below this point"]]}

blocks.text: Some fields also use deciles, splitting data into 10 equal parts, or percentile ranks in single-point steps, all built from the exact same underlying percentile machinery, just at a different resolution.
5. The Interquartile Range

The interquartile range, or IQR, is Q3 minus Q1, the width of the middle 50 percent of the data. It measures spread the same way standard deviation does, but using only rank position, which makes it inherit the same outlier resistance the median has.
A small IQR relative to the overall range signals that most of the data clusters tightly in the middle, while a large IQR signals genuinely spread out, variable data.
6. Using the IQR to Detect Outliers

A widely used rule flags any value more than 1.5 times the IQR below Q1, or above Q3, as a potential outlier. This threshold, unlike a standard deviation based rule, does not assume the data is normally distributed, making it a safer default for skewed or unusual distributions.

code.content:
lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
outliers = [x for x in data if x < lower_bound or x > upper_bound]
print(outliers)

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: For exam scores with Q1 at 60 and Q3 at 85, the IQR is 25, so any score below 22.5 or above 122.5 would be flagged as an outlier, a wide, forgiving band that only catches genuinely extreme values.

blocks.text: The 1.5 multiplier is a widely used convention, not a strict mathematical law, some analyses use a stricter 3 times multiplier specifically to flag only the most extreme values as outliers.
7. Percentile Ranks: The Reverse Direction

A percentile rank asks the opposite question from a percentile: given a specific value, what percentage of the dataset falls below it. This is exactly what many standardized test score reports show a student directly.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
score = 78
rank = stats.percentileofscore(data, score)
print(rank)   # what percent of the dataset this score beats

blocks.text: Percentile and percentile rank are inverse operations, one goes from a percentage to a value, the other goes from a value back to a percentage, and confusing the direction of the question being asked is a common source of errors.
8. Box Plots: Visualizing Percentiles

A box plot draws a box from Q1 to Q3, with a line at the median, and whiskers extending to the smallest and largest non-outlier values, giving a compact, five-number visual summary of a dataset shape and spread all at once.

blocks.alt: A box plot built from percentiles
blocks.caption: The box spans Q1 to Q3, the line marks the median, whiskers show the non-outlier range

blocks.text: Points plotted individually beyond the whiskers on a box plot are exactly the outliers the IQR rule from section 6 would flag, making a box plot a fast visual way to spot them without computing anything by hand.
9. Percentiles in AI Systems: Latency

Machine learning inference systems almost always report latency using percentiles rather than a plain average, since a single slow outlier request can hide inside an average while still badly affecting real users. p50 gives the typical response time, while p95 and p99 reveal how bad the worst experienced delays actually are.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Meaning"],"rows":[["p50","the median response time, what a typical request experiences"],["p95","95 percent of requests are faster than this"],["p99","99 percent of requests are faster than this, exposing the worst tail behavior"]]}

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A model serving system with a mean latency of 50 milliseconds can still have a p99 latency of 800 milliseconds, meaning 1 percent of users experience a response 16 times slower than average, a problem the mean alone completely hides.

blocks.text: Service level agreements for production machine learning systems are almost always written in terms of a percentile latency target, such as p99 under 500 milliseconds, rather than an average target, precisely because averages hide the tail behavior users actually notice.
10. Robust Feature Scaling with Percentiles

Rather than scaling a feature using its mean and standard deviation, which the standard deviation lesson noted are sensitive to outliers, a robust scaler instead uses the median and the IQR, subtracting the median and dividing by the IQR, giving a scaling approach that outliers barely disturb.

code.content:
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[10], [12], [11], [13], [1000]])   # one extreme outlier
scaled = RobustScaler().fit_transform(X)
print(scaled)

blocks.text: This is directly analogous to the standardization idea from the standard deviation lesson, subtract a center, divide by a spread, just built from rank based statistics that outliers cannot meaningfully distort.
11. Percentile-Based Versus Standard Deviation Based Outlier Detection

The standard deviation lesson covered flagging outliers as anything more than a few standard deviations from the mean, but that approach assumes a roughly normal distribution, exactly the assumption the empirical rule depends on. The IQR based rule from section 6 makes no such assumption, making it the safer default whenever a dataset skewness or shape is unknown or clearly non-normal.

When in doubt about a dataset shape, the IQR based rule is generally the more conservative, broadly applicable default, while the standard deviation based rule remains a reasonable choice once normality has actually been checked and confirmed.
12. Percentiles in Evaluation Metrics

Beyond raw latency, percentiles show up throughout model evaluation whenever a single average would hide important tail behavior, reporting the 95th percentile of prediction error across a test set, for example, alongside the mean error, reveals how badly the model performs on its worst cases, not just on average.

code.content:
import numpy as np
errors = np.abs(np.random.randn(1000) * 2)
print(np.mean(errors), np.percentile(errors, 95))   # the p95 error is typically much larger than the mean

blocks.text: A model with a low average error but a high p95 error is likely failing badly on a specific, identifiable subset of cases, worth investigating separately rather than assuming the model is uniformly reliable.
13. Percentile Binning for Feature Engineering

Converting a continuous feature into discrete groups based on percentile boundaries, quartile bins for instance, is a common feature engineering technique, useful when a model benefits more from a rough rank position than from the exact raw value, or when the raw value has a highly skewed, hard to model distribution.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
data = pd.Series([12, 45, 23, 67, 34, 89, 21, 56])
quartile_bins = pd.qcut(data, q=4, labels=["low", "mid-low", "mid-high", "high"])
print(quartile_bins)

blocks.text: Because each bin is defined by percentile boundaries rather than fixed width ranges, every bin ends up with roughly the same number of data points, avoiding the sparse or overcrowded bins a fixed width scheme can produce on skewed data.
14. A Worked Example
A company records response times, in milliseconds, for 10 customer support chats: 200, 220, 210, 900, 205, 215, 230, 195, 208, 225. Compute Q1, the median, Q3, and check for outliers.

code.content:
data = [200, 220, 210, 900, 205, 215, 230, 195, 208, 225]
q1 = np.percentile(data, 25)
median = np.percentile(data, 50)
q3 = np.percentile(data, 75)
iqr = q3 - q1
upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(q1, median, q3, iqr, upper_bound)
print([x for x in data if x > upper_bound])   # flags the 900 outlier

blocks.text: The single 900 value stands out clearly once the IQR based bound is computed, even though a quick glance at the mean alone might not make it as obvious how unusual that one chat truly was compared to the rest.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing a percentile with a plain percentage score, being in the 90th percentile does not mean scoring 90 percent correct, it means beating 90 percent of the comparison group.
Applying the 1.5 times IQR outlier rule blindly without checking whether the flagged points are genuine data errors or simply valid, rare extreme values worth keeping.
Using a standard deviation based outlier rule on clearly skewed data, when the IQR based rule from section 6 is the more appropriate, assumption-free choice.
Reporting only average latency for a system, hiding exactly the kind of tail behavior that p95 and p99 from section 9 are specifically designed to reveal.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: assuming every value flagged by the 1.5 times IQR rule is necessarily an error to remove, some flagged values are genuine, important extreme events that deserve investigation rather than automatic deletion.
16. Practice: Compute Quartiles and Detect Outliers
Given the dataset [5, 7, 8, 6, 9, 200, 7, 8, 6, 9], compute Q1, Q3, the IQR, and identify any outliers using the 1.5 times IQR rule.

code.content:
data = [5, 7, 8, 6, 9, 200, 7, 8, 6, 9]
q1, q3 = np.percentile(data, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print([x for x in data if x > upper])

blocks.text: Compare the mean of this dataset against its median once the 200 outlier is included, and notice how much further the mean gets dragged away from the typical values than the median does, echoing the same lesson from the median chapter.
Key Takeaway

The evaluation metrics module later in this curriculum returns to percentile based reporting in more depth, since summarizing a model performance with a single average number is rarely enough to catch how it behaves in its worst, tail cases.

A percentile describes relative position within a sorted dataset, generalizing the median, the 50th percentile, into a full family of position markers. Quartiles and the interquartile range built from percentiles give an outlier detection method and a robust scaling method that make no assumption about the shape of the underlying data.

Percentiles reappear constantly in applied AI work, from latency monitoring using p50 and p99 to robust feature scaling before model training, making this lesson a practical bridge between classical descriptive statistics and everyday machine learning systems engineering.

This lesson closes out the four classic ways to summarize a single column of data, mean, median, mode, and percentiles, each offering a different, complementary lens on where values sit and how spread out they are.
